text: Tonight, you'll probably eat something hot.
Rice. Bread. Curry. Maybe just a fried egg.
You won't even think about it.
But no other animal on Earth does this.
Not one.
So why do we?
Rewind two million years.
Our ancestors ate everything raw.
Leaves. Fruit. Roots. Raw meat, when they could get it.
And raw food has a problem.
It's tough. It takes forever to chew.
A chimpanzee spends around six hours a day just chewing.
Six hours. Every single day.
You spend about one.
And here's the strange part.
Raw food doesn't only cost time. It hides its energy.
Eat a raw egg, and your body absorbs only about half of its protein.
Cook that same egg, and it absorbs over ninety percent.
Fire unlocked food.
That mattered because of one hungry organ.
Your brain.
It's about two percent of your body weight, but it burns around twenty percent of your energy.
An ape eating raw leaves can't easily feed a brain like that.
But a cook can.
The oldest clear trace of fire used by humans comes from Wonderwerk Cave, in South Africa.
Ash and burnt bone, about one million years old.
Some scientists, like Richard Wrangham at Harvard, think cooking started even earlier, and that it changed our bodies.
Smaller teeth. A smaller gut. A bigger brain.
Others say the evidence isn't strong enough yet. That debate is still going on.
But there's one clue that's hard to ignore.
In a German study of people who ate only raw food, most lost weight.
And nearly a third of the women stopped having regular periods.
Their bodies simply weren't getting enough energy.
We don't just like cooked food.
We may not be built to live without it.
So tonight, when you light the stove, remember what you're really doing.
You're repeating the trick that turned a chewing ape into you.
